name: Monotonic Stack
description: Maintain a stack that's always increasing or always decreasing in value, used to efficiently find the next/previous greater or smaller element for every position in an array in a single pass.
core_technique: Iterate through the array, and while the current element violates the stack's monotonic order (e.g. is greater than the stack's top for a next-greater-element problem), pop from the stack and resolve the popped element's answer using the current element - then push the current element.
common_pitfalls: Pushing values instead of indices - most problems need the index (to compute distance, e.g. 'days until warmer') not just the value; forgetting elements that never get popped simply have no answer (e.g. no greater element to their right) and need a default value (-1, 0, or similar depending on the problem); confusing whether the stack should be increasing or decreasing for the specific variant (next-greater vs next-smaller flips the direction).

example_problems.title: Daily Temperatures
example_problems.why_it_fits: For each day, find how many days until a warmer temperature -- maintain a decreasing stack of indices; when a warmer day appears, pop and compute the distance for each popped index.

example_problems.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
example_problems.why_it_fits: For each bar, find the nearest shorter bar on both sides to determine the widest rectangle it can anchor -- an increasing stack of indices resolves both boundaries in one pass.

example_problems.title: Next Greater Element I
example_problems.why_it_fits: Direct application -- decreasing stack of values/indices, popped whenever a greater element is found, giving each element's next greater in O(n) total instead of O(n^2) brute force.

additional_considerations: Always verify each element is pushed and popped at most once -- this is what gives the O(n) total complexity despite the nested-looking while loop, and it's worth stating explicitly since the amortized analysis isn't obvious at first glance. For histogram-style problems, pushing a sentinel value (height 0) at the end forces all remaining bars in the stack to be resolved, which avoids a separate cleanup loop.
